passages.t: Jonathan's covenant, and a song Saul could not bear
passages.happening:
“After David had finished speaking with Saul, the souls of Jonathan and David were knit together, and Jonathan loved him as himself” (verse 1). Saul keeps David at court from that day (verse 2).

“Then Jonathan made a covenant with David because he loved him as himself” (verse 3). He takes off his robe and gives it to David, with his tunic, his sword, his bow and his belt (verse 4).

David succeeds in everything Saul sends him to do, and Saul puts him over the fighting men. The people are pleased, and so are Saul's officers (verse 5).

When the army comes home, the women come out from every town with singing, dancing and tambourines (verse 6). As they dance, they sing, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands” (verse 7). Saul is furious. “They have ascribed tens of thousands to David,” he said, “but only thousands to me. What more can he have but the kingdom?” (verse 8). ‘And from that day forward Saul kept a jealous eye on David’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Almost everyone in this chapter loves David: Jonathan, Michal, all Israel and Judah, even Saul's servants. Saul alone fears him.

Jonathan's gift was more than generosity. Clothes and weapons could stand for a person's identity and position. The crown prince's robe on David's shoulders is a striking picture of Jonathan handing over what would have been his.

A covenant here means a binding promise sworn between two people, often with duties reaching to their families. This one will be renewed twice more, and David will keep it long after Jonathan's death. The word love was also used in that world for the loyalty between allies, and that sense sits beside the personal affection in this chapter.

Women's victory songs, with dancing and tambourines, were the usual welcome for warriors coming home. The pairing of thousands with tens of thousands is a normal pattern of Hebrew poetry, which rises from one number to a larger one for emphasis. Saul hears it as a ranking.

His question, ‘What more can he have but the kingdom?’, shows that he already fears for his throne. Samuel had told him that the kingdom would go to a neighbor better than he. Now Saul has someone to watch.
passages.later:
The women's welcome had happened before: ‘Then Miriam the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women followed her with tambourines and dancing’ (Exodus 15:20).

David remembered Jonathan in his lament after Jonathan's death: “I grieve for you, Jonathan, my brother. You were delightful to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women” (2 Samuel 1:26). And as king he kept the covenant with Jonathan's family: “Is there anyone left from the house of Saul to whom I can show kindness for the sake of Jonathan?” (2 Samuel 9:1).
passages.hard:
What kind of love did Jonathan have for David?

The chapter says that Jonathan loved David ‘as himself’, and some modern readers ask whether the relationship was romantic or sexual. The long-standing Jewish and Christian reading, held by most commentators, sees a deep friendship and covenant loyalty. It points out that the words for love and covenant in this chapter are also the words of political alliance, and that nothing in the text describes a sexual relationship. Some modern interpreters argue that the language here, and David's lament in 2 Samuel 1:26, suggest a romantic bond.

Readers should know that both readings exist, and weigh them against the text itself. What the chapter shows beyond doubt is covenant love that seeks the other's good at great cost. Jonathan, the heir to the throne, hands his robe and his weapons to the man God has chosen instead of him.
passages.asks: Jonathan gave David the robe that marked him as heir. Ask whose success you are glad of, and whose you resent, as Saul did. And ask what it would cost you to love someone ‘as yourself’ when their rise means your loss.

passages.t: A spear, and the LORD with David
passages.happening:
The next day a spirit of distress from God comes on Saul, and he prophesies inside the house while David plays the harp as usual. Saul is holding a spear, and he hurls it, thinking, “I will pin David to the wall” (verse 11). David gets away from him twice.

“So Saul was afraid of David, because the LORD was with David but had departed from Saul” (verse 12). Saul sends him away and gives him command of a thousand men (verse 13). David leads them out to battle and back, ‘and he continued to prosper in all his ways, because the LORD was with him’ (verse 14).

When Saul sees how successful David is, he is afraid of him. ‘But all Israel and Judah loved David, because he was leading them out to battle and back’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is built on two short statements repeated again and again: the LORD was with David, and Saul was afraid. Saul's fear grows in stages. David's success is told four times.

The word for David's success means both acting wisely and prospering. It is not luck. It is skill joined to God's presence. In Hebrew it sounds almost like the word Samuel used when he told Saul he had acted foolishly in chapter 13. The wise one and the foolish one are set side by side.

Saul's plan to get rid of David by sending him away backfires. Command of troops makes David loved by all Israel and Judah. Every scheme Saul makes moves David forward.

The phrase ‘leading them out to battle and back’ is exactly what the people wanted a king to do in chapter 8. They wanted a king to go out before them and fight their battles. David is doing it, and Saul is not.
passages.later: The wisdom books know the power of the feeling that drives Saul: “Wrath is cruel and anger is like a flood, but who can withstand jealousy?” (Proverbs 27:4).
passages.asks: Saul's jealousy began with a song. Ask what small thing has started a jealousy in you, and where it could lead if you let it grow. And ask what it would mean to be glad when the LORD is with someone else.

passages.t: Saul's daughters, and a deadly bride-price
passages.happening:
Saul offers David his elder daughter Merab, if David will fight the LORD's battles. Saul's real thought is that the Philistines will kill him (verse 17). David answers, “Who am I, and what is my family or my father’s clan in Israel, that I should become the son-in-law of the king?” (verse 18). When the time comes, Merab is given to another man (verse 19).

‘Now Saul’s daughter Michal loved David’ (verse 20), and Saul is pleased. “I will give her to David,” Saul thought, “so that she may be a snare to him” (verse 21). He sends his servants to tell David privately that the king is pleased with him (verse 22). David says he is a poor man who cannot pay a king's price (verse 23).

Saul names his price: no dowry but proof that a hundred Philistines have been killed, ‘But Saul intended to cause David’s death at the hands of the Philistines’ (verse 25). Before the time is up, David and his men kill two hundred Philistines and bring the proof the king demanded. Saul gives him Michal as his wife (verses 26-27).

When Saul sees that the LORD is with David and that Michal loves him, ‘he grew even more afraid of David. So from then on Saul was David’s enemy’ (verse 29). David's name becomes highly honored (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
A bride-price, mohar in Hebrew, was paid by the groom to the bride's family. David, a poor man, could not pay what a king would ask. Saul turns the custom into a trap. The price he names is grim, a hundred dead Philistines with the proof of it, and the chapter tells it in two verses without lingering.

The narrator lets the reader see Saul's plans, ‘let the hand of the Philistines be against him’, while David speaks only of his own unworthiness. Saul is the only person in the chapter whose thoughts are told, and they are schemes.

Michal is the one person in the chapter whose love is said to please someone for the wrong reason. Her father welcomes it because he thinks it can be used against the man she loves.

And again Saul's scheme backfires. The Philistine test was meant to kill David. It makes him the king's son-in-law and part of the royal family, which gives him a place close to the throne and also a place within Saul's reach.

Merab's marriage to Adriel is mentioned again in 2 Samuel. The oldest Greek manuscripts are shorter in this chapter, as in the last, and lack the offer of Merab. Scholars disagree about whether the longer Hebrew or the shorter Greek is closer to the earliest form. The shape of events is the same in both.
passages.later:
The law describes the custom Saul twisted: a man who takes a young woman as wife ‘must pay the full dowry for her to be his wife’ (Exodus 22:16).

Years later David will demand Michal back, reminding her brother of this price: “Give me back my wife, Michal, whom I betrothed to myself for a hundred Philistine foreskins” (2 Samuel 3:14).
passages.hard:
Saul uses his own daughter's love as a trap, and sets a bride-price meant to get David killed. What does the chapter make of this?

The chapter shows it, and does not admire it. The narrator opens Saul's thoughts so that the reader sees the plan for what it is: a father using his daughter as bait, and a king trying to have his own champion killed without raising his hand. David says nothing against Saul, only that he is unworthy. Michal's love is real, and her father treats it as a tool.

The price itself is told plainly and briefly. The chapter does not hold it up as a pattern, and it does not linger on it. Its interest is elsewhere: every plan Saul makes against David ends by moving David forward, because the LORD is with him.
passages.asks: Saul treated his daughter's love as a tool. Ask whether you have ever used someone's love or loyalty to get what you wanted. And ask whom you could protect from being used that way.
